title: Health
body:
בריאות וחיים

Bri’ut Ve’Chayim

Health remains one of the most serious challenges affecting many families within the Nasenyi Jewish Community. Limited financial resources, long travel distances, poor access to medical services, and inadequate nutrition continue to affect the wellbeing of both children and adults throughout the community.
For many families, reaching a health facility can already be difficult. The cost of transportation, medical consultations, diagnostic tests, and medicines often places proper healthcare beyond reach. As a result, illnesses that could be treated early sometimes become more severe before help is received.

Donate Now

Children are especially vulnerable to these conditions. Many walk long distance each day to access education, traveling through heavy rain, mud, and intense sun, often without adequate meals. These hardships affect not only their physical health, but also their strength, concentration, growth, and ability to learn effectively. Yet despite these difficulties, they continue pursuing education with remarkable determination and resilience.
Nutrition remains another major concern within the community. Some families struggle to provide consistent and balanced meals, particularly during periods of economic hardship. In this context, communal meals during Shabbat, festivals, and gatherings become more than moments of fellowship they also become moments of nourishment, care, and relief for many children and families.Elders and vulnerable members of the community also face significant challenges related to healthcare access, ongoing treatment, and transportation to medical facilities. Even so, the spirit of care within Nasenyi remains strong. 

Health and Life

Families check on one another, visit the sick, share what they can, and continue offering emotional and spiritual support during times of illness and difficulty.
Health in Nasenyi is understood as more than physical wellbeing alone. Emotional strength, spiritual encouragement, dignity, community support, and human connection are all considered essential parts of healing and wellbeing. In difficult moments, people continue turning toward one another with compassion, prayer, and hope.
Despite limited resources, the community continues striving for a healthier future for its children and families. The resilience of the people, together with the kindness of friends and supporters near and far, continues to strengthen hope within the community.
Our hope is to improve access to healthcare, nutrition, medicine, health education, and support for vulnerable families and children so that future generations may grow in healthier and more stable conditions.
In Nasenyi, caring for health means caring for life, dignity, and the future of the community itself.

title: Study & Learning
body:
לימוד וחכמה

Limud Ve’Chokhmah

Learning is one of the deepest values within the Nasenyi Jewish Community. Through study, prayer, storytelling, and shared teaching, we continue to preserve Jewish faith, strengthen community identity, and pass knowledge from one generation to the next.

Children, youth, and adults all take part in learning community life. Young members of the community are introduced to Hebrew prayers, Torah stories, Jewish values, and festival traditions from an early age. Learning often happens not only through formal lessons, with youth sharing with younger ones what they know, but also through participation in worship, communal gatherings, songs, and celebrations that bring faith to life.

Our community has already taken an important step by building a Beit Midrash– a house of study dedicated to Torah learning and spiritual growth.

Donate Now

Learning and Wisdom

Life in Nasenyi is built around people. Around families gathering after prayer, children playing beside elders, neighbors supporting one another, and a community that continues to remain united through both joy and hardship.
Our synagogue is more than a place of worship. It is where friendships are strengthened, meals are shared, stories are told, and people find comfort, belonging, and encouragement. Long after prayers end, people often remain together speaking, laughing, learning, and simply enjoying the presence of one another. These moments of togetherness are at the heart of community life in Nasenyi.
Children are deeply woven into every part of communal life. They grow up surrounded by songs, prayer, celebration, storytelling, and the guidance of parents and elders who continue passing traditions from one generation to the next. Their energy fills our gatherings with life and hope for the future.

For us, this space represents hope, commitment, and the desire to create a stronger future for the next generation. However, despite having the structure, the Beit Midrash still remains unequipped. We currently lack many of the essential learning materials needed for proper study, including Jewish books, siddurim, Hebrew learning resources, desks, educational materials, and other basic equipment for children and students.
Many of our children face difficult conditions in order to access education. Some walk distances of more than 9 kilometers to school and another 9 kilometers back home each day. They travel under heavy rain and intense sun, and many do so on empty stomachs. Yet despite these hardships, they continue pursuing both secular and Jewish learning with determination, resilience, and hope for a better future.
Our desire to deepen Torah study continues to grow, even while facing serious challenges. The community currently has limited access to trained teachers, rabbinic guidance, and educational resources. We also do not have a resident rabbi to guide advanced Torah learning or answer questions concerning Jewish law and practice.

These challenges are especially felt in relation to our Torah scrolls. One of our smaller Torah scrolls was damaged by insects beyond repair, while the handle of our larger Torah scroll is broken, making it difficult to use properly during study and worship. Without proper rabbinic guidance, we remain uncertain about their condition and kosher status, yet we continue to preserve them with great care and reverence because they remain sacred to our community.
Despite all these difficulties, the spirit of learning in Nasenyi remains strong. 

Learning and Wisdom

In Nasenyi, learning is more than education alone. It is a path toward faith, dignity, opportunity, and continuity. Through study, we strengthen not only knowledge, but the future of our entire community.Families continue gathering to study Torah portions, children continue learning prayers and songs, and the community remains committed to preserving Jewish knowledge and identity for future generations.

title: Our History
body:
Nasenyi

Jewish Community

A vintage photo of Semei Lwakirenzi Kakungulu.

Through the influence of his political office, he ordered all the chiefs in his palace and outside to be circumcised. 

In 1919, he started the Abayudaya community as a religion. He taught the chiefs how to lead prayers in their local language which was “Luganda” and other ceremonies in their respective areas of origin.

Many synagogues were built such as Namanyonyi Nabugoye, Namakole, Nasenyi, Kabwangasi, Putti, Namutumba, etc. using his resources. Kakungulu died on the 24th/Nov/1928 . The chiefs went ahead to lead those synagogues in their respective places.

Although these community leaders did not have much formal education, they observed the Jewish culture and beliefs like observing Shabbat, Jewish festivals, circumcision of male babies at 8 days, the law of Niddah, and a lot more. 

Mishael Birogi who worked as a house helper to a British water engineer in Mbale region in the 1950s found out that his boss Joseph (whose last name is unknown) was Jewish from how both sanctified Shabbat.

Mishael Birogi praying.

Consequently, Mishael became the first person to read and write Hebrew language in the history of the Abayudaya. He was given some elementary Hebrew books a portable Chumash which he used to teach other members in the community. Many members went through his hands including Gershom Sizomu who later became a Rabbi for Nabugoye Synagogue.

The population grew to over 3000 followers by 1970.

 In 1971, the government of Uganda was overthrown by the dictator, Idi Amin Dada who banned other religions including Judaism (Abayudaya). “We suffered and starved to worship and serve our God,” Abraham a member in the Nasenyi community remarked.

Local leaders were ordered to close or break down all synagogues and continued hunting any members worshiping openly to be arrested. This period resulted in many members converting to other religions like Islam and Christianity in fear for their lives.

Zakayo Fuma Balozi sitting in his courtyard.

Mweru Daniel picked up from Wamani Enosh after his death and he led in prayers,  read the torah in Luganda, gave weekly d’var Torah.

At the age of 67, Daniel is currently working as a gatekeeper at Hadassah Primary School. He no longer serves as a spiritual leader since he did not acquire formal rabbinic education. He isn’t fluent in English language or Hebrew.

Nasenyi

Jacob Mwosuko.

The history of the Abayudaya contains many individuals who quietly sustained Jewish life through dedication, sacrifice, and community leadership. Among them is Jacob Mwosuko, whose contributions span youth education, community leadership, communal support, music, and land donation for Jewish worship.

About Nasenyi

A Living Jewish Community in Uganda

The Nasenyi Jewish Community – Makor Chayim is one of the oldest Abayudaya communities in Uganda, with roots dating back to 1923. Our story is part of a remarkable Jewish journey that began with Semei Kakungulu and has endured through persecution, isolation, and generations of faithful community leadership.

Today, our synagogue remains a spiritual home where families gather for Shabbat, festivals, Torah study, communal meals, and mutual support. Hebrew prayers rise alongside Luganda melodies, reflecting a Jewish identity that is both deeply rooted and uniquely Ugandan.

The people who preserved our faith

Jacob Mwosuko.

As the first chairman of the Abayudaya Jewish community, He led the community in a very challenging period. This was the aftermath of the Amin regime as fear was still instilled in the community members following the ban of other religious beliefs except Islam and Christianity. This was a period of disrupted continuity in Ugandan Judaism and an effort to bridge and reunify the community.

” I remember one day when my father Wamani Enosh, a teacher at Nasenyi synagogue, was banned from burying his member who died,” recounts Jacob. “We were chased away and my father ran into a nearby house for his safety. “I ran and hid in the swamp, and we left the body unburied and without prayer,” he added.

Some few consistent members who preserved Judaism in Nasenyi and Uganda at large during this regime prayed indoors. They could close the doors and pray under a low tone or in silence with someone watching outside.

However, he steered the community towards re-unity, through personal sacrifices, encouragement of the youth, socially, economically among others.

A Ugandan Seder: Passover 2026 in Nasenyi

 Sweet, textured, and uniquely ours. It wasn’t just a substitute; it felt like a discovery. Honestly, it must have been the best.

This beautiful night was made possible because the people of the Nasenyi community gave from the heart. Everyone contributed in their own way so that we could have a true communal meal one where no one was left out, and everyone belonged. And beyond our community, support also came from our precious friends from far away. Though distant in place, they were present with us in spirit, on our table, and in our joy.

To all of you who supported us—we thank you.
You made this day unforgettable.

There was a softness to the whole evening. A sweetness. You could see it in the smiles that didn’t fade, in the way people lingered, in the warmth that stayed even in silence. This day truly put a smile on everyone.

And in the middle of it all, without needing to announce it, we lived the words: “Hineh ma tov u’ma na’im”– how good and how pleasant it is for people to dwell together in unity.

This was not just about remembering the Shemot (Exodus)

It was about belonging.
About taking an ancient story and letting it breathe in our language, our food, our clothing, our laughter.

I would say this was the best, not because everything was perfect, but because everything was real, Sweet, joyful, and completely ours.

At 71 years old, Lyaga Damali continues to ride nearly ten kilometers by bicycle every week to attend Shabbat prayers. She has lived through persecution, illness, and poverty, yet her devotion has never faded.

“Every kilometer she rides is an act of devotion.”

Her story reflects the resilience of the entire Nasenyi community—faith carried forward through extraordinary perseverance.

title: The 8 Kilometers of Faith
body:
The Story of Lyaga Damali

Mama Damali is a remarkable woman from the Nasenyi Jewish Community who kept her faith alive during Uganda’s difficult times under Idi Amin, when many hid their identity. Today, she lives alone in a tiny, leaky house she shares with goats, battling ulcers, high blood pressure, and pain from a hernia surgery—yet she still rides her bicycle 8 to 10 kilometers every week to attend Shabbat prayers, a journey the community calls “The 8 Kilometers of Faith.” Despite her extreme poverty, darkness, and failing health, she never complains, only prays with humility and hope, asking for a simple, dignified home on her own land and a motorcycle to ease her travel and earn a little income. Her story is not about suffering, but about unwavering faith, quiet strength, and the beautiful resilience of a woman who refuses to let go of God or her community, no matter what life brings.

Watch video

At 71 years old, Lyaga Damali continues to live a life shaped by faith, resilience, and extraordinary perseverance.

During the years of the Idi Amin regime, when fear and persecution caused many people to abandon or hide their Jewish identity, Mama Damali remained among the very few who continued holding onto the faith. In Kabwangasi Synagogue, she became the only known survivor who preserved that spiritual connection through those difficult years. Today, she carries not only her own story, but also part of the memory and survival of Jewish life within the region.

Mama Damali lives alone in Kabwangasi, Gosei Cell, without children or close family members to care for her. The nearest synagogue to her home is Nasenyi Synagogue, located approximately 8 to 10 kilometers away. Yet every week, despite age, illness, and physical pain, she rides her bicycle to attend Shabbat prayers.

Within the community, her journey has become known as:

“The 8 Kilometers of Faith.”

She lives with ulcers, high blood pressure, and severe pain resulting from a hernia surgery that greatly weakened her health. During cold weather, the pain around the surgery area becomes especially difficult, particularly while riding long distances on her bicycle. Yet she continues coming to pray whenever she is physically able, holding firmly to her belief that Hashem gives healing, strength, and life.
Her living conditions remain extremely difficult.
Mama Damali currently lives in a small house that she shares with livestock, including goats. At night, the animals remain inside the same living space, creating severe discomfort and making it difficult for her to breathe and rest properly. The animals urinate inside the house during the night, and the conditions continue affecting both her health and wellbeing.
The house itself is in poor condition. The roof leaks heavily during rainstorms, exposing her to cold and wet conditions inside her home. She has no electricity and no proper lamp, leaving her to spend many nights in darkness.
Yet despite all this, she continues choosing faith.
In the video, Mama Damali speaks with humility and sincerity about her greatest hopes. She asks for help to build a simple home where she can live with dignity, safety, and peace. She already has land where a small house could be constructed if support became available. For her, such a home would not represent luxury, it would represent rest, health, and the ability to live her remaining years in humane conditions.

She also explains that receiving a motorcycle would greatly change her life. It would ease the difficult journey to and from the synagogue for prayers, especially during times of pain and illness. Beyond transportation, she believes the motorcycle could also help her generate small income and support her daily survival, giving her greater independence and stability.
What makes Mama Damali’s story so powerful is not only the hardship she faces, but the spirit with which she continues living. She does not speak with bitterness. She speaks with faith.
In many ways, her journey reflects the spirit of the Nasenyi Jewish Community itself humble, resilient, faithful, and determined to continue despite hardship.
Every kilometer she rides is an act of devotion.
Every Shabbat she attends is a testimony of perseverance.
And every prayer she joins carries the strength of a woman whose faith refused to disappear even in the hardest of times.

title: Festivals & Celebrations
body:
מועדים ושמחה

Mo’adim Ve’Simchah

Festivals & Celebrations

In Nasenyi, the Jewish festivals are more than dates on a calendar. They are seasons that gather the community together in prayer, reflection, celebration, memory, and hope. Throughout the year, sacred days transform the rhythm of community life, filling the synagogue and homes with song, learning, warmth, and togetherness.
As each festival approaches, preparations begin throughout the community. Families gather, children become excited, prayers are practiced, and the atmosphere slowly changes with anticipation. Hebrew prayers blend naturally with Luganda melodies, creating celebrations that are deeply Jewish while also reflecting the life and spirit of our Ugandan home.
The joy of the children becomes one of the most memorable parts of the evening during the search for the afikomen. Laughter fills the room as they search eagerly from corner to corner, refusing to give up until it is finally found. Those moments fill the entire community with happiness and turn the Seder into a living memory shared by all generations.

Donate Now

Mo’adim Ve’Simchah

Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur bring a quieter and more reflective spirit into the community. As the shofar is sounded, families gather in prayer, repentance, and hope for the new year ahead. These sacred days invite the community to reflect deeply, seek renewal, strengthen faith, and pray for life, peace, health, and blessing in the year to come.
Sukkot also carries special meaning within Nasenyi. Although obtaining important ritual items such as the lulav and etrog is often very difficult, the longing to observe the mitzvot of the festival remains strong. The effort required to celebrate these traditions only deepens their meaning and reminds the community how precious Jewish observance truly is.

מועדים ושמחה

Mo’adim Ve’Simchah

Hanukkah fills the community with warmth, light, and joy. As candles are lit each evening, families gather to remember perseverance, faith, and the enduring strength of Jewish life. Children sing songs, stories are shared, and the glow of the menorah brings beauty and hope into the community during the festival season.

In Nasenyi, the festivals are not only remembered—they are lived with full hearts, carried with devotion, and passed lovingly from one generation to the next.

Learning is one of the deepest values within the Nasenyi Jewish Community. Through study, prayer, storytelling, and shared teaching, we continue to preserve Jewish faith, strengthen community identity, and pass knowledge from one generation to the next.

Children, youth, and adults all take part in learning community life. Young members of the community are introduced to Hebrew prayers, Torah stories, Jewish values, and festival traditions from an early age. Learning often happens not only through formal lessons, with youth sharing with younger ones what they know, but also through participation in worship, communal gatherings, songs, and celebrations that bring faith to life.

Our community has already taken an important step by building a Beit Midrash– a house of study dedicated to Torah learning and spiritual growth.

title: Global Connection
body:
קשר עולמי

Kesher Olami

Though Nasenyi is a small community in Uganda, our story reaches far beyond our borders. Across different countries, languages, and cultures, we remain connected to a wider Jewish world through friendship, faith, learning, and shared humanity.
For our community, these connections are deeply meaningful. In a place where many important Jewish resources are difficult to access locally, support from friends and communities abroad has helped sustain both spiritual and communal life. Matzah for Passover, lulav and etrog for Sukkot, siddurim, books, educational materials, and other sacred items have often reached Nasenyi through the kindness of people who chose to stand with us despite the distance between us.

Donate Now

Global Connection

These gestures carry meaning far beyond the physical items themselves. A box of matzah, a prayer book, or a message of encouragement reminds the community that we are not forgotten that somewhere across the world, others care about the survival and growth of Jewish life in Nasenyi.
Global connection has also strengthened learning, friendship, and cultural exchange within the community. Visitors, teachers, supporters, and friends from different parts of the world have helped encourage Torah study, preserve traditions, and deepen understanding of Jewish life and practice. These relationships continue to build bridges between communities that may live far apart geographically, yet remain connected spiritually and humanly.
At the same time, Nasenyi also shares something unique with the wider world. Our community reflects a living expression of Judaism shaped by Ugandan culture, communal warmth, resilience, and faith. Hebrew prayers rising together with Luganda songs, festivals celebrated with local traditions, and the spirit of togetherness within the community all form part of a Jewish identity that is both rooted and distinctive.

Kesher Olami

Even in times of hardship, these global relationships continue to strengthen hope within the community. They remind us that Jewish life can flourish even in small and distant places when people choose solidarity, compassion, and connection over isolation.

What makes these connections truly powerful is that they are built not only on assistance, but on mutual respect, friendship, and shared belonging. Communities separated by oceans and continents continue to recognize one another as part of one people and one shared story.

In Nasenyi, global connection means more than reaching across the world, it means knowing that even with great distances, hearts can still remain close.

title: About Us
body:
Nasenyi

A Living Jewish Community

” The Abayudaya, whose name means ” People of Judah” in Luganda are a Ugandan Jewish Community that identifies with people and follows Jewish religious traditions. It started as a religion by Semei Kakungulu a British agent who was sent to concur the Eastern Uganda territories. Kakungulu read the bible and discovered that there was only one God not 3 (Trinity) as it’s believed by the Christian. He therefore converted himself to Judaism.

Donate Now

1919 — The Beginning of the Abayudaya

Through the influence of his political office, he ordered all the chiefs in his palace and outside to be circumcised. 

In 1919, he started the Abayudaya community as a religion. He taught the chiefs how to lead prayers in their local language which was “Luganda” and other ceremonies in their respective areas of origin.

Many synagogues were built such as Namanyonyi Nabugoye, Namakole, Nasenyi, Kabwangasi, Putti, Namutumba, etc. using his resources. Kakungulu died on the 24th/Nov/1928 . The chiefs went ahead to lead those synagogues in their respective places.

Although these community leaders did not have much formal education, they observed the Jewish culture and beliefs like observing Shabbat, Jewish festivals, circumcision of male babies at 8 days, the law of Niddah, and a lot more. 

Mishael Birogi who worked as a house helper to a British water engineer in Mbale region in the 1950s found out that his boss Joseph (whose last name is unknown) was Jewish from how both sanctified Shabbat.

Mishael Birogi praying.

Consequently, Mishael became the first person to read and write Hebrew language in the history of the Abayudaya. He was given some elementary Hebrew books a portable Chumash which he used to teach other members in the community. Many members went through his hands including Gershom Sizomu who later became a Rabbi for Nabugoye Synagogue.

The population grew to over 3000 followers by 1970.

 In 1971, the government of Uganda was overthrown by the dictator, Idi Amin Dada who banned other religions including Judaism (Abayudaya). “We suffered and starved to worship and serve our God,” Abraham a member in the Nasenyi community remarked.

Local leaders were ordered to close or break down all synagogues and continued hunting any members worshiping openly to be arrested. This period resulted in many members converting to other religions like Islam and Christianity in fear for their lives. Many Jewish cultures and beliefs were abandoned, including Shabbat. “You could work up to Thursday and rest on Fridays, then work on Saturday and rest on Sunday”. Moses, another member of Nasenyi Community said. 

1979–2001

Rebuilding Jewish Life in Uganda

Following years of persecution and isolation, the Abayudaya community began the long journey of rebuilding Jewish life across eastern Uganda. Nasenyi emerged once again as one of the communities that preserved faith, memory, and communal identity through extraordinary resilience.

Timeline block From 1979

1979 — Freedom Returns

In 1979, the dictatorship of Idi Amin came to an end, and religious communities across Uganda were once again free to worship openly. For the Abayudaya, this marked the beginning of a new chapter after years of fear, secrecy, and loss.

1980–1982 — Searching for the Surviving Communities

Abayudaya youth began traveling from synagogue to synagogue to discover which Jewish communities had survived the years of persecution. Poor roads, limited transportation, and broken communication made the journey difficult, yet they continued searching with determination.

They found that some congregations had disappeared entirely, while others had survived quietly through the faithfulness of only a few families who continued praying indoors.

Donate Now

“The community chose not only to survive, but to rebuild.”

Timeline block from 1986

1986 — A Community Reunited

A general Abayudaya gathering was held at Nabugoye, where community leaders reorganized Jewish life in Uganda and elected new leadership. This meeting symbolized unity, renewal, and the determination to preserve Judaism for future generations.

1995 — Reconnecting with World Jewry

Through connections made in Nairobi, the Abayudaya were introduced to Kulanu, an American Jewish organization. International friendships began to end decades of isolation and brought new opportunities for education, healthcare, safe water, and Jewish learning.

Timeline block from 2001

The Founding of Nasenyi Synagogue

 Founded by Semei Kakungulu in 1923, the synagogue was first led by Zakayo Fuma Balozi as its spiritual leader. He was later succeeded by Enosh Wamani, who continued to guide the community through prayer, Torah study, and communal leadership. Nasenyi Synagogue has remained a vibrant center of Jewish faith and tradition, where Shabbat and festival observances, 

2001 — A New Era of Jewish Renewal

In 2001, a Beit Din of Conservative rabbis visited Uganda and formally converted many members of the Abayudaya community according to Conservative Jewish practice. This became one of the most significant moments in the modern history of Ugandan Judaism and strengthened the community’s connection with the wider Jewish world.

Nasenyi Synagogue, located in Bwikomba Village II, Mugiti Sub-county, Budaka District, is one of the oldest Abayudaya synagogues in Uganda. It was established by Semei Kakungulu in 1923, with Zakayo Fuma Balozi serving as its first spiritual leader. He was later succeeded by Enosh Wamani, who continued guiding the community through prayer, Torah reading, and communal leadership.

For more than a century, Nasenyi has remained a place where Jewish life is lived through Shabbat, festivals, Hebrew prayer, Luganda song, and the unwavering commitment of generations who refused to let their traditions disappear.

Zakayo Fuma Balozi sitting in his courtyard.

Mweru Daniel picked up from Wamani Enosh after his death and he led in prayers,  read the torah in Luganda, gave weekly d’var Torah.

At the age of 67, Daniel is currently working as a gatekeeper at Hadassah Primary School. He no longer serves as a spiritual leader since he did not acquire formal rabbinic education. He isn’t fluent in English language or Hebrew.

The history of the Abayudaya contains many individuals who quietly sustained Jewish life through dedication, sacrifice, and community leadership. Among them is Jacob Mwosuko, whose contributions span youth education, community leadership, communal support, music, and land donation for Jewish worship.

The people who preserved our faith

Jacob Mwosuko.

As the first chairman of the Abayudaya Jewish community, He led the community in a very challenging period. This was the aftermath of the Amin regime as fear was still instilled in the community members following the ban of other religious beliefs except Islam and Christianity. This was a period of disrupted continuity in Ugandan Judaism and an effort to bridge and reunify the community.

” I remember one day when my father Wamani Enosh, a teacher at Nasenyi synagogue, was banned from burying his member who died,” recounts Jacob. “We were chased away and my father ran into a nearby house for his safety. “I ran and hid in the swamp, and we left the body unburied and without prayer,” he added.

Some few consistent members who preserved Judaism in Nasenyi and Uganda at large during this regime prayed indoors. They could close the doors and pray under a low tone or in silence with someone watching outside.

However, he steered the community towards re-unity, through personal sacrifices, encouragement of the youth, socially, economically among others.

 

Donate Now

The Early Kibbutz Camp in Nasenyi (Late 1980s)

Historical accounts from community members attribute one of the earliest Abayudaya kibbutz-style youth camps to the late 1980s, shortly after the difficult years of rebuilding Jewish life in Uganda.

The first camp was organized in Nasenyi, where Jacob Mwosuko warmly opened his home to the youth of the community. For several days and nights, young Abayudaya gathered there to live, learn, and practice Jewish communal life.

During this camp:

  • Youth slept and stayed at Jacob Mwosuko’s home.
  • Campfires were lit in the evenings, creating a communal environment for discussion and study.
  • Shabbat was observed collectively, strengthening the rhythm of Jewish religious life.
  • Participants engaged in Torah study and Hebrew learning, helping transmit Jewish knowledge to a younger generation.

This informal but structured communal experience resembled the kibbutz model, emphasizing shared living, learning, and work for the benefit of the community.

Personal Sacrifice and Support of the Kibbutz Youth

Jacob Mwosuko personally sustained the youth during this period, feeding them from the crops he cultivated on his own land.

The foods he provided included staples grown locally such as:

Cassava, sweet potatoes, beans, maize grains, millet, wheat and other seasonal farm produce.

Even after the Nasenyi camp ended, his support did not stop.

 

The journey from Nasenyi to Nabugoye Hill is roughly 15–20 kilometers, depending on the route. Riding this distance with sacks of raw harvested food required significant endurance, especially on rural roads and hills. Yet Jacob repeatedly made these trips to ensure the kibbutz youth and community members had food.

He would harvest food from his fields, load it onto a bicycle, and ride to Nabugoye Hill, one of the main centers of the Abayudaya community near Mbale.

Support for Jewish Education

Jacob Mwosuko’s contributions extended to educational institutions within the Abayudaya community.

For several years he supplied food to Jewish schools without cost, including:

Hadassah Primary School and Semei Kakungulu High School.

This food support helped sustain students and school activities during periods when resources were limited.

Jacob Mwosuko also participated in the preservation and presentation of Abayudaya Jewish music.

He is credited as a vocalist on the internationally released album:

Abayudaya: Music from the Jewish People of Uganda

The recording was produced by Smithsonian Folkways Recordings in 2003, and it introduced Abayudaya liturgical music to a global audience. Jacob Mwosuko performed Psalm 93, contributing his voice to a recording that helped document and preserve the musical traditions of the community.

Donation of Land for the Nasenyi Synagogue

 Another major contribution by Jacob Mwosuko concerns the development of Jewish infrastructure in Nasenyi.

He donated several acres of his personal land for the construction of the Nasenyi Jewish synagogue, ensuring that the community would have a permanent place for prayers, learning, development and gatherings.

In 2025, he formalized this commitment by preparing a legal document transferring ownership of the land to the Nasenyi Jewish community. The document officially records the donation and was received by the community leadership board, confirming the land’s status as communal property dedicated to Jewish religious use.

Nasenyi Abayudaya community home to approximately 500 Jews thrives on subsistence farming. With many of her members semi-illiterate, like most of the people in the Bukedi sub region, over 99.5% of Nasenyi members live under $1 a day. , UBOS, 2023). It is not uncommon for some families in this Jewish community to go without meals for days in certain seasons because we depend on nature to grow our food crops .

Currently Nasenyi synagogue sits on 3.5 acres which was donated by a community member. Despite the number of Jews in Nasenyi, we do not have a trained Rabbi for over 100 years now. So, all Jewish ceremonies including but not limited to Bar and Bat Mitzvot are carried out by volunteer spiritual leaders and self-trained Hazanot; this is because efforts to get a member trained have never yielded. “We dream of the day we shall have a Chuppah celebrated in the Nasenyi Jewish community,” says Emunah one of the youths in the community. Nasenyi members dream of the day they will have a Bait Midrash and Library full of Hebrew and Judaic resources. We still have hope that one day one of our members will get a chance to be trained as rabbi so we can get the guidance and be taught on what, how and when to do some things.

 Nasenyi and Abayudaya at large have a problem of recognition. Judaism in Uganda is still seen as a new foreign religion though it has been in existence for over 100 years. Jewish high holidays and festivals are not recognized on the calendar of Uganda. This makes teaching very difficult to children who learn from non-Jewish schools or not in school at all. It also hurts that our own country doesn’t recognize our presence and so does Israel.

Nasenyi synagogue has no electricity. This challenge has greatly affected Kabbalat Shabbat and other evening prayers before festivals.

Inadequate safe water supply; Nasenyi community happens to have only one safe water borehole with a manual water pump and serves about 1,600 people in the village regardless of religion. The borehole isn’t currently functioning due to the failed pump so we get water from unprotected and unsafe water sources which exposed many residents to water borne, water related, and water-wash diseases.

Long distances to quality education and high costs; the only Jewish schools that may teach Judaism and Torah are very far and expensive to afford therefore children end up joining non-Jewish private or government schools founded by either Christianity or Islam according to one’s affordability with or without a dish of lunch and water. Our children only have a few weeks to learn the little Judaism and Hebrew from parents at home since there’s no shul or Rabbi to teach. The Poor kids from poor Jewish homes never get chance to read or even write.

 The difficulty in accessing health services has negatively impacted the quality of life of the women and children in this community. We have registered several preventable deaths and illnesses due to inadequate knowledge, inaccessible and affordable health services in this community.

Poor food harvests have been a routine because members have no access to paste-resistant and fast-growing seed varieties coupled with no agricultural mechanization or irrigation technologies. This has resulted in food insecurities and malnutrition (commonly in children) among the members of the Nasenyi Abayudaya community.

To improve the socioeconomic status of the members of the Nasenyi community, there should be a deliberate effort to equip and empower members with the skills to engage in activities for empowerment and sustainability such as Agriculture-processing, farm inputs, Hospitality businesses like Kosher Restaurant and guest house that can accommodate visitors.

 This can give confidence to our visitors from abroad as they would be living with brothers and sisters.

In conclusion, though Nasenyi community is one of the strong participants and contributors to the entire Abayudaya development, it has lagged behind in terms of development. There’s a need of quick intervention to rescue the children who walk long distances in search of education, treatment, water and other essential services. This will break this vicious circle of poverty that’s faced by Nasenyi community.

Chinuch Ve’Atid

At Nasenyi Synagogue, heritage and preservation are essential to keeping our faith, culture, and traditions alive for future generations. The synagogue serves as a living connection between the past, present, and future of the community.
Through worship, education, music, language, and traditional practices, we honor the rich history of Jewish life while ensuring that younger generations understand and appreciate their identity and values.

Heritage and Preservation

What makes preservation in Nasenyi remarkable is that it continues even through hardship. Limited access to Torah resources, Jewish books, ritual items, and religious guidance has not stopped the community from praying, learning, celebrating, and passing traditions forward. Instead, these challenges have strengthened the community’s determination to protect and preserve its heritage with dignity and devotion.
The friendship and support of people from around the world have also become part of this journey. Sacred items, educational materials, encouragement, and acts of kindness from friends abroad continue helping sustain Jewish life within the community and remind us that even distant communities remain connected as one people.
In Nasenyi, preservation is not about protecting the past from disappearing. It is about keeping faith, identity, memory, and tradition alive so that future generations may continue to inherit them with pride, dignity, and hope.

title: Honoring the Legacy of Aaron Kintu Moses
body:
Aaron Kintu Moses

He was admired for his humility and generosity. Many remember him as someone who always made time for others, whether offering guidance to young people, supporting struggling families, welcoming visitors, or encouraging members of the community to remain strong in their faith and identity. His kindness and calm spirit earned him deep respect both within Uganda and abroad.

Donate Now

Honoring the Legacy of Aaron Kintu Moses

Aaron Kintu Moses was a respected educator, mentor, community builder, and devoted supporter of Jewish life in Uganda. He was a prominent member of the Abayudaya, a unique Jewish community located mainly in eastern Uganda around Mbale.

For many people, Aaron was more than a leader. He was a source of encouragement, wisdom, and hope. He dedicated his life to serving others, strengthening his community, and ensuring that future generations would grow up with education, dignity, faith, and opportunity.

Aaron Kintu Moses served as the founding director and headmaster of Hadassah Primary School, where he worked tirelessly to provide quality education to children from different backgrounds. Under his leadership, the school welcomed Jewish, Christian, and Muslim students alike, reflecting his belief that education should unite people and uplift communities.

Honoring the Legacy of Aaron Kintu Moses

Aaron also played an important role in sharing the story of the Abayudaya with the wider world. Through conversations with visitors, partnerships with international Jewish organizations, speaking engagements, and educational work, he helped introduce many people around the world to the history, traditions, and resilience of the Abayudaya community. His sincerity and wisdom helped build lasting friendships between Ugandan Jews and the international Jewish community, bringing support and recognition to many local projects and schools.

At the same time, Aaron believed strongly in honesty, accountability, and transparency in leadership. In his later years, he and several of his brothers openly raised concerns about the management of certain community properties and institutions. He believed that strong communities must be built on truth, fairness, and responsibility, even when difficult conversations are required. His willingness to speak openly about these issues reflected the courage of a man who cared deeply about the future of his people.

You can hear Aaron Kintu Moses speaking about some of these community matters here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bgpe0hE2kcI

Aaron Kintu Moses also showed great kindness and encouragement to smaller Jewish communities, including the Nasenyi community. Although he was not a member of Nasenyi, he cared deeply about its growth and future. Through his encouragement, mentorship, and friendship, he inspired many people working to strengthen Jewish learning, community organization, and religious life in the area.

Those who knew Aaron remember not only his leadership, but the warmth of his character. He believed deeply in the power of education, the importance of faith, and the responsibility of serving others. His life reflected quiet strength, compassion, and unwavering dedication to his community.

Aaron Kintu Moses passed away on September 11, 2020. His passing was deeply felt throughout the Abayudaya community and among friends around the world. Yet his legacy continues through the schools he helped build, the students he inspired, the communities he strengthened, and the many lives he touched.

The Nasenyi Jewish Community – Makor Chayim remembers Aaron Kintu Moses with deep gratitude and respect. His wisdom, encouragement, and example continue to inspire our commitment to faith, learning, unity, and community service.

זיכרונו לברכה —Zichrono Livracha— May his memory be a blessing.

title: Food Security & Farming
body:
מזון ואדמה

Mazon Ve’Adamah

Despite these hardships, the spirit of resilience within Nasenyi remains strong. Families continue planting, cultivating, harvesting, and sharing what they can with one another. During difficult seasons, community members support neighbors and vulnerable families however possible, reflecting the strong culture of mutual care that continues to define life in Nasenyi.
Farming is also closely tied to community life and celebration. title: Sukkot 2026 in Nasenyi: Celebrating in Our Sukkahs
body:
Sukkot 2026 in Nasenyi: Celebrating in Our Sukkahs, Home by Home

Sukkot 2026 brought a different kind of celebration to Nasenyi Jewish Community. There was no large communal meal, no elaborate community gathering, and this year we did not have a lulav and etrog. Yet throughout Nasenyi, there was something beautiful to see:

Sukkahs were everywhere.

Across the community, families built sukkahs at their homes. Almost every household had its own sukkah — some simple, some more carefully decorated, but each one representing the same desire to observe and celebrate this special Jewish festival.

For several days, these temporary shelters became places of prayer, eating, conversation, laughter and family togetherness.

Bringing Sukkot Into Our Homes

Sukkot reminds us of the temporary dwellings associated with the Israelites’ journey through the wilderness and of our dependence upon God even when the structures around us may seem uncertain.

In Nasenyi, that message became something people could see and experience right outside their homes.

Families gathered inside their sukkahs to eat and spend time together. Friends visited one another. People sat, talked and enjoyed the festival in these temporary spaces.

Some members of our community went even further and spent nights sleeping inside their sukkahs, wanting to experience the mitzvah in a particularly personal way.

When night came, these sukkahs were not simply decorations standing beside people’s homes. For some families, they became living spaces — places where people ate, gathered, rested and slept.

It gave Sukkot in Nasenyi a beautiful simplicity.

Celebrating Without a Lulav and Etrog

This year, our community did not have a lulav and etrog, important ritual items traditionally used during Sukkot.

We certainly felt their absence.

But their absence did not stop Sukkot.

Rather than allowing what we did not have to define the festival, families celebrated with what was available to them. They built their sukkahs, gathered inside them and observed the festival as best they could.

For Nasenyi, this became another reminder that limited resources do not have to mean the disappearance of Jewish life.

Sometimes Jewish life is sustained simply because people decide that a tradition matters enough to continue.

A Different Celebration This Year

Unlike some of our other festivals and community celebrations, we were not able to organize a communal Sukkot meal this year because the community did not have the funds to do so.

Naturally, we would have loved to bring everyone together around one table.

But Sukkot still happened.

We observed the two festival days. Families gathered in their own sukkahs. People ate together at home, visited one another and enjoyed the time they could spend inside the temporary shelters they had built.

In an unexpected way, the absence of a large communal celebration made this year’s Sukkot particularly personal.

Instead of one sukkah becoming the centre of the celebration, the community itself seemed to become a collection of sukkahs.

Home after home had built one.

Family after family found its own way of observing.

And throughout Nasenyi, Jewish life continued.

Our Sukkahs Tell a Story

There is something powerful about seeing so many sukkahs standing beside ordinary homes in Nasenyi.

They tell the story of a community that may not always have everything it needs, but continues to practise its Judaism with commitment and joy.

We did not have the lulav and etrog.

We did not have the resources for a large communal meal.

But we had our sukkahs.

We had our families.

We had one another.

And we had the determination to celebrate.

For some, Sukkot meant eating a meal inside the sukkah. For others, it meant sitting there with family and friends and enjoying conversation. And for those who chose to spend the night inside, it meant falling asleep beneath the temporary covering of a sukkah they had built with their own hands.

Perhaps that is what will make Sukkot 2026 particularly memorable in Nasenyi.

It was not defined by how much we had.

It was defined by how much we were willing to do with what we had.

As the festival came to an end, the sukkahs standing throughout Nasenyi remained a quiet testimony to something important about our community: Jewish life here is not confined to the synagogue or to large celebrations.

It lives in our homes. It lives in our families. And sometimes, it lives beneath the simple roof of a sukkah built beside a home in Nasenyi.

Chag Sukkot Sameach from Nasenyi Jewish Community.

title: Yom Kippur in Nasenyi: Fasting, Faith and Rain at the End of a Sacred Day
body:
Yom Kippur in Nasenyi: Fasting, Faith and Rain at the End of a Sacred Day

Yom Kippur this year was a deeply meaningful day for the Nasenyi Jewish Community — a day of prayer, repentance, fasting, togetherness and gratitude.

From the beginning, the community was beautifully transformed by white.

Women arrived dressed in beautiful white dresses, while the men wore elegant white kanzu. Together, the congregation created a remarkable scene of simplicity, dignity and unity as we gathered for one of the holiest days of the Jewish year.

The kanzu is a traditional long garment worn by men in Uganda, particularly during important religious, cultural and family occasions. Usually reaching towards the ankles, it represents dignity and respect. Seeing our men worshipping in white kanzu gave Yom Kippur in Nasenyi a character that was both deeply Jewish and beautifully Ugandan.

A Fast That Tested Our Strength

As beautiful as the day was, it was not an easy one.

Yom Kippur requires us to put aside many of our ordinary physical comforts and turn our attention towards repentance, prayer and our relationship with God and one another. For those who were able to fast, the long hours without food or water became increasingly challenging as the day continued.

By the later hours, some members were extremely hungry, thirsty and weak. A few wondered whether they would have enough strength to reach the end.

Others seemed remarkably strong and continued through the day with energy, encouraging those who were struggling.

Yet whether strong or exhausted, we remained together.

There was something powerful about seeing people continue praying even when their bodies were tired. The hunger and thirst reminded us that Yom Kippur is not simply another gathering on the Jewish calendar. It asks something from us. It gives us time to examine ourselves, seek forgiveness, forgive others and consider the kind of people we want to become in the year ahead.

And Then the Rain Came

As the long day finally approached its end, something beautiful happened in Nasenyi.

The rain began to fall.

After spending the day fasting — with some members having struggled greatly with thirst — we reached the end of Yom Kippur with rain falling around us.

Then came the moment everyone had been waiting for:

We broke the fast.

There was an indescribable sweetness in that first drink and the first taste of food after such a demanding day. Those who had felt weak slowly regained their strength. Tired faces turned into smiles. Conversation returned. People ate together, laughed together and reflected on the day we had just completed.

Outside, the rain continued to fall.

We did not need to give the rain a special meaning to appreciate the beauty of the moment. After a long, dry day of fasting, ending Yom Kippur surrounded by the sound of rainfall while sharing food together was simply unforgettable.

A Gift of Love from Friends Far Away

The beautiful breaking of the fast was made possible through the generosity of Rabbi Jeremy Gerber of Congregation Beth El in Edison, New Jersey, who funded the food and refreshments enjoyed by the community.

His generosity meant that after the long hours of fasting, our members could sit together and end the sacred day with a proper meal.

But what reached Nasenyi was more than financial support.

It was love.

Although many kilometres and an ocean separate Nasenyi from New Jersey, acts such as these remind us that Jewish community can reach far beyond geography. Rabbi Jeremy’s continued friendship and care have helped our community experience the knowledge that somewhere far away, there are people who know Nasenyi, think about Nasenyi and want to see our Jewish life continue to grow.

To Rabbi Jeremy Gerber and our friends at Congregation Beth El, we extend our heartfelt gratitude. Your kindness helped make this Yom Kippur possible and enabled our community to conclude this sacred day together with food, happiness and dignity.

Jewish in Faith, Ugandan at Heart

Perhaps one image will remain with us when we remember this Yom Kippur:

Our women dressed beautifully in white.

Our men standing together in their white Ugandan kanzu.

A community praying together.

Some strong, others tired and thirsty, but still together.

And finally, after the long hours of fasting, rain falling over Nasenyi as families and friends gathered to break the fast.

It was a beautiful meeting of Jewish faith, Ugandan culture, community and friendship.

Yom Kippur reminded us that community is not only about celebrating together when things are easy. It is also about enduring together, praying together, encouraging the person beside us when they are struggling, and finally sitting at the same table when the difficult journey is complete.

The fast ended.

The rain fell.

Food was shared.

Strength returned.

And another Yom Kippur in Nasenyi became part of our community’s story.

May we carry its lessons with us throughout the year — seeking forgiveness where we have caused hurt, offering forgiveness where we have been hurt, caring for one another and continuing to build a community rooted in faith, kindness and love.

G’mar Chatimah Tovah — May we all be sealed for a good year.

The Rosh Hashanah 5787 celebration reflected an important part of the identity of the Nasenyi Jewish Community: a community deeply rooted in Jewish faith while proudly embracing its African heritage.

The celebration brought Jewish prayer and traditions together with Ugandan culture, clothing, food, friendship, and community.

Jewish Faith at the Centre

Prayer was central to the celebration.

Members of the community gathered for communal prayers as they welcomed the new Jewish year.

The occasion provided a time for faith, reflection, gratitude, and fellowship.

Proudly African

Alongside Jewish traditions, the celebration also reflected the community’s African heritage.

On the first day, many members dressed beautifully for the festival.

On Sunday, some members wore traditional African clothing.

Men wore the kanzu, while women, including Damali Lyaga, wore the Ugandan traditional dress known as the gomesi.

Bringing Traditions Together

The combination of Jewish prayer and African attire created a memorable celebration.

Food, friendship, prayer, Jewish tradition, and African culture all came together as members celebrated the new year.

This combination reflects the distinctive identity of Nasenyi Jewish Community.

A Memorable Celebration

Rosh Hashanah 5787 provided an opportunity for the community to celebrate its faith while also embracing its African heritage.

The celebration demonstrated that Jewish tradition and African cultural identity can be expressed together within the life of the Nasenyi community.

title: Rosh Hashanah 5787 at Nasenyi Jewish Community
body:
Celebrating the Jewish New Year — September 2026

Rosh Hashanah 5787 was a joyful and meaningful celebration for the Nasenyi Jewish Community—a time of prayer, gratitude, togetherness, and hope for the year ahead.

Our preparations began modestly, with a single contribution from one of our community members. From that small beginning, more support followed. We were blessed to receive generous contributions from Rabbi Jeremy, Kulanu Inc., AMC Farm, and members of our own community. Each contribution, whether large or small, helped bring life to our Rosh Hashanah celebration.

The first day of Rosh Hashanah coincided with Shabbat, and because of the timing of our Kabbalat Shabbat preparations and services, we were unable to organize the larger communal meal we had hoped for. We therefore extended our main community gathering to Sunday, the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

On Sunday, September 13, the community gathered once again for communal prayers, followed by a beautiful shared meal prepared by RVD Events, whose members are also part of the Nasenyi Jewish Community.

The celebration brought together people of different ages. Members of the Jewish community were joined by some of our non-Jewish neighbours and local children, sharing in the happiness and hospitality of the occasion. Most importantly, everyone who joined us was able to enjoy a plate of food and experience the warmth of celebrating together.

Celebrating Our Jewish Faith and African Heritage

Our Rosh Hashanah celebration also reflected the unique identity of our community—deeply rooted in Jewish faith while proudly embracing our African heritage.

On the first day, many members came dressed beautifully for the festival. On Sunday, some continued this spirit through traditional African attire. Men wore the kanzu, a traditional long garment commonly worn in Uganda and East Africa, while women, including Damali Lyaga, wore the elegant Ugandan traditional dress known as the gomesi.

The combination of prayer, Jewish tradition, African dress, food, friendship, and community made the second day of Rosh Hashanah particularly memorable.

Our Gratitude

On behalf of the Nasenyi Jewish Community, we extend our sincere appreciation to Kulanu Inc. for the generous contribution of UGX 260,000, which gave an important boost to our preparations and helped make the communal celebration possible.

We also extend our heartfelt gratitude to Rabbi Jeremy for his support and generosity, and to AMC Farm for standing with our community and lending us a much-needed helping hand.

Above all, we thank every member of the Nasenyi Jewish Community who contributed money, time, food, preparation, prayer, service, or simply their presence.

Community is built when each person recognizes that even a small contribution can become part of something much greater.

We encourage our members to continue with this spirit of participation, generosity, and shared responsibility as we work together for the growth and success of our community.

As we begin 5787, may the new year bring peace, good health, unity, provision, and renewed strength to our community, our friends, our supporters, and all those who have stood with us.

Shanah Tovah U’Metukah — שנה טובה ומתוקה!

May it be a good and sweet new year.

title: Beyond Water Filters: Nasenyi’s Need for a Sustainable Water Solution
body:
The distribution of 40 water filters to families in the Nasenyi Jewish Community has provided important and immediate relief.

However, the intervention has also highlighted a much larger challenge facing the community: the need for a reliable and sustainable source of safe water.

Immediate Relief for 40 Families

On 2 September 2026, Mighty Water provided 40 water filters to the Nasenyi Jewish Community through Simcha Katalima.

The filters were distributed to 40 families, giving them an additional way to treat water collected from alternative sources.

Simcha also provided practical training on how to assemble, use, and care for the filters.

For the families who received them, the support is meaningful and timely.

But the Water Challenge Continues

Nasenyi continues to depend largely on one functioning borehole.

During prolonged drought, the borehole can struggle to meet the needs of the many people who depend on it. Heavy consumption can cause the available water supply to become depleted.

When this happens, families have to look elsewhere for water.

Some alternative sources may not always provide water of dependable cleanliness, making water treatment an important concern.

A Long-Term Solution Is Needed

Water filters can help families treat water from alternative sources, but they cannot replace a reliable community-wide water supply.

The long-term need for Nasenyi is therefore much greater.

The community needs a sustainable source of safe water that can serve families consistently, including during prolonged periods of drought.

Such a solution would reduce the pressure on the existing borehole and provide families with greater security and confidence in their access to water.

An Opportunity to Make a Lasting Difference

The recent support from Mighty Water and Simcha Katalima shows the positive impact that partnerships can have on the lives of families in Nasenyi.

The 40 filters have provided immediate assistance.

The next step is finding sustainable solutions that address the root of the community’s water challenge.

We are deeply grateful to Mighty Water, Simcha Katalima, and everyone who has supported the Nasenyi Jewish Community.

The need remains, but so does our hope for a future where every family in Nasenyi can access safe and reliable water.

title: Why Safe Water Remains a Challenge for the Nasenyi Jewish Community
body:
For many communities, access to water is something that can easily be taken for granted. For the Nasenyi Jewish Community, however, reliable access to safe water remains an ongoing challenge.

The community currently depends largely on one functioning borehole, which serves a large number of people.

The Impact of Prolonged Drought

The challenge becomes more serious during prolonged periods of drought.

With limited water available and many families depending on the same borehole, heavy consumption can cause the available supply to become depleted.

When the borehole cannot provide enough water, families are left with few alternatives.

They may have to search for water from other sources, even when the cleanliness and safety of those sources cannot always be guaranteed.

The Importance of Water Treatment

This situation makes water treatment particularly important.

The recent donation of 40 water filters from Mighty Water, delivered through Simcha Katalima, has provided some families with an additional way to treat water collected from alternative sources.

The filters do not eliminate the wider water challenge, but they provide practical support to the 40 families who received them.

Teaching Families How to Use the Filters

The distribution was accompanied by practical training.

Simcha Katalima demonstrated how to assemble, use, and care for the filters, giving families the knowledge needed to use them properly.

This was an important part of the intervention because access to water-treatment equipment is most useful when families understand how to operate and maintain it correctly.

The Bigger Challenge

Although the filters have brought relief, Nasenyi’s water challenge remains.

The community needs a reliable and sustainable water source capable of serving families throughout the year, particularly during prolonged drought.

Safe water is essential for the health, dignity, and well-being of every family.

Standing With Nasenyi

The Nasenyi Jewish Community is grateful to everyone supporting efforts to improve access to safe water.

The recent distribution of water filters demonstrates what can be achieved through community support and partnership.

However, the long-term goal remains to find a sustainable solution that will ensure that families in Nasenyi can access safe and reliable water even during the most difficult periods.

Helping During Difficult Times

When water from the borehole becomes unavailable or insufficient, families may have to collect water from other sources.

The donated filters provide an additional way for families to treat such water before use.

A Heartfelt Thank You

The Nasenyi Jewish Community extends its sincere appreciation to Mighty Water and Simcha Katalima for their generosity and commitment to supporting families in Nasenyi.

The 40 filters have brought immediate relief to the families who received them.

At the same time, this support highlights the larger need for a dependable water solution for the entire community.

title: The Strength of Community: How Nasenyi Families Support One Another
body:
The story of the Nasenyi Jewish Community is not only a story of faith and worship. It is also a story of people coming together to support one another through everyday challenges.

For generations, families in Nasenyi have built a strong sense of community around shared Jewish values, traditions, and responsibility for one another.

Standing Together in Difficult Times

During such moments, the strength of a community becomes especially important.

The recent distribution of 40 water filters is one example of how support can reach families when they need it most. The filters provided immediate assistance to families facing difficulties accessing reliable water.

Faith and Community Responsibility

Jewish tradition places strong importance on caring for others and supporting those in need.

At Nasenyi, these values are reflected in the way community members come together during times of difficulty, celebrations, worship, and other important moments.

The synagogue provides a place where people can pray together, learn together, and strengthen relationships.

Building a Stronger Future

A strong community is built when people look beyond their individual needs and work toward the well-being of everyone.

For Nasenyi, this means continuing to support children through education, improving access to basic services, strengthening livelihoods, and preserving Jewish traditions.

Every act of support contributes to this larger goal.

A Community With Hope

Nasenyi continues to face challenges, but the community remains committed to building a better future.

With continued cooperation between community members, local leaders, supporters, and partners, there is an opportunity to create lasting improvements for families and future generations.

The strength of Nasenyi is ultimately found in its people—the families, leaders, children, and supporters who continue to stand together.

title: From a Short Visit to a Lasting Friendship
body:
Sometimes, a short visit can create memories that last for many years.

This was the experience of the Nasenyi Jewish Community when David Yair and Itai Mayar from Israel visited us from Friday, 7 August to Sunday, 9 August 2026.

They came as visitors.

They left as friends.

How the Connection Began

The story began earlier in the year with Noam, who had previously visited the Nasenyi community.

Through that connection, David and Itai later learned about Nasenyi and were connected with the community through Jonathan Mwosuko, who received them and helped bring them to us.

What began as a simple connection eventually became a meaningful Jewish encounter.

Sharing More Than a Visit

During their time at Nasenyi, David and Itai did much more than visit the synagogue.

They spent time with our children.

They taught Hebrew.

They shared Israeli songs and games.

They participated in Shabbat.

David read from the Torah in Hebrew.

Both guests shared Divrei Torah with the congregation.

And throughout their visit, they interacted warmly with members of the community.

These moments helped create a feeling of family.

One Jewish Family

Nasenyi is part of the Abayudaya Jewish community of Uganda, a Jewish community whose members maintain Jewish religious and cultural life in eastern Uganda. The Abayudaya communities have developed relationships with Jewish communities and organizations around the world, helping create opportunities for learning, exchange, and strengthening Jewish identity.

David and Itai’s visit was another example of how these connections can bring people together.

Israel and Uganda may be separated by thousands of kilometres, but during those few days, the distance felt much smaller.

We shared Torah.

We shared Hebrew.

We shared songs.

We shared laughter.

We shared Shabbat.

The Children Will Remember

Perhaps one of the most meaningful parts of the visit was the time David and Itai spent with the children.

For the children, meeting visitors from Israel was not simply a lesson.

It was an experience.

They could see, hear, play, and learn with people who came from another Jewish community.

Those memories can encourage curiosity and strengthen their sense of belonging to the wider Jewish world.

The Beginning of Something More

David and Itai’s visit lasted only three days, but friendship does not have to be measured in days.

The relationships created through visits, learning, and shared Jewish experiences can continue long after the visitors return home.

We hope that this visit is only the beginning of a lasting friendship between David, Itai, and the Nasenyi Jewish Community.

We thank them for their kindness, their teachings, their time with our children, and their friendship.

Todah Rabbah, David and Itai.

Our doors will always be open to you.

Until we meet again — להתראות! 🇮🇱❤️

title: Torah, Hebrew and Understanding at Nasenyi Jewish Community
body:
At Nasenyi Jewish Community, Torah is central to our Jewish life.

Our services, learning, and community activities are shaped by the desire to understand Jewish tradition and pass it on to the next generation.

Our recent Shabbat with David Yair and Itai Mayar from Israel gave us an opportunity to reflect on how we approach Torah reading, Hebrew, and Jewish education.

Hebrew and the Language of the Community

Hebrew has an important place in Jewish worship.

It is the language in which much of our prayers and Torah are traditionally expressed. For this reason, learning Hebrew is an important part of Jewish education at Nasenyi.

At the same time, our community is located in Uganda, where Luganda is widely used in everyday communication.

This creates an interesting and meaningful combination.

During our Torah service, we normally read the first Aliyah in Hebrew and continue the remaining Aliyot in Luganda.

Why We Use Luganda

The use of Luganda is not because Torah is less important to us.

Quite the opposite.

We want people to understand what they are hearing.

If the congregation hears every Aliyah in Hebrew without understanding its meaning, some of the message can become inaccessible.

By using Luganda, we allow more members of the congregation to follow the Torah reading and participate in the learning.

This reflects one of the values that is important to our community: Jewish learning should be shared.

The Need for Hebrew Education

At the same time, we recognize the importance of increasing access to Hebrew education.

Nasenyi continues to work toward strengthening Jewish education for children and adults. Access to Hebrew learning materials, teachers, and opportunities to interact with Hebrew speakers can make a significant difference.

This is why visits such as David and Itai’s are so valuable.

During their visit, they taught children Hebrew, Israeli songs, and games. Their interaction gave the children an opportunity to experience Hebrew in a living and enjoyable way.

The wider Jewish community has also supported educational development in Nasenyi. In 2025, the Jewish Educators Assembly and USCJ reported providing approximately 25 boxes of Jewish educational materials, including Hebrew language resources and Torah study guides.

Learning Together

The goal is not to choose between Hebrew and Luganda.

The goal is to create a community where people can hear Torah in Hebrew, understand its meaning in a language they know, and continue developing their Hebrew skills.

For us, Torah is not only something to read.

It is something to learn, understand, teach, and live.

Our Shabbat with David and Itai reminded us of the beauty of this journey and the importance of continuing to strengthen Jewish education at Nasenyi.

title: David Reads from the Torah During Shabbat Service at Nasenyi
body:
A particularly memorable moment took place during the Shabbat service at Nasenyi Jewish Community on Saturday, 8 August 2026.

David Yair, one of our guests from Israel, was invited to read from the Torah.

For the congregation, it was a special opportunity to hear the Torah read fluently in Hebrew by a visitor from Israel.

A Moment of Torah and Connection

The Torah stands at the heart of Jewish life.

At Nasenyi, Torah reading is an important part of Shabbat worship and community learning. The service brings together prayer, Hebrew, Torah, and the participation of the entire congregation.

When David was invited to read, he accepted the opportunity and read beautifully.

His Hebrew reading added a special dimension to the service and created a moment of connection between the Nasenyi community and Jewish life in Israel.

Hebrew and Luganda in Our Torah Service

Nasenyi has developed a way of conducting Torah reading that helps the entire congregation participate.

Normally, the first Aliyah is read in Hebrew, while the remaining Aliyot are continued in Luganda.

This approach reflects an important value within our community: understanding.

While Hebrew remains central to Jewish prayer and Torah, the congregation should also be able to understand the message being shared.

For this reason, Luganda helps make the Torah accessible to members who may not yet have advanced Hebrew knowledge.

Our limited access to highly trained Hebrew and rabbinic teachers has also influenced this practice. At the same time, it represents our desire to ensure that Torah is not something people simply hear without understanding.

Strengthening Hebrew Learning

David’s reading also reminded us of the importance of continuing to develop Hebrew education within Nasenyi.

The community has a strong desire to strengthen Jewish learning among its children and members. External partnerships and visits from Jewish communities around the world can help create valuable opportunities for this growth.

The broader Abayudaya community has long maintained a blend of Hebrew and local languages in Jewish worship and learning.

A Memory We Will Keep

David’s Torah reading was more than a part of the Shabbat service.

It was a moment of connection.

A Jewish visitor from Israel stood before a Jewish congregation in Nasenyi, Uganda, and shared the ancient words of Torah in Hebrew.

It reminded us that Torah can connect Jewish communities across continents.

We are grateful to David for sharing this special moment with us.

title: Israeli Guests Teach Hebrew to Nasenyi Children
body:
For the children of Nasenyi Jewish Community, the visit of David Yair and Itai Mayar was an exciting opportunity to learn, play, sing, and interact with guests from Israel.

David and Itai visited Nasenyi from Friday, 7 August to Sunday, 9 August 2026. During their short stay, they dedicated time to the children and introduced them to Hebrew, Israeli songs, and games.

Learning Hebrew Through Friendship

Hebrew is an important part of Jewish religious and cultural life.

At Nasenyi, children encounter Hebrew through prayer, Torah, songs, and Jewish learning. However, opportunities to interact directly with Hebrew speakers can make the language feel much more alive and accessible.

David and Itai brought this experience directly to the children.

Instead of learning only from books, the children were able to hear Hebrew, repeat words, sing songs, play games, and interact with people from Israel.

The result was both educational and enjoyable.

Learning Beyond the Classroom

The visit demonstrated that Jewish education does not happen only inside a classroom.

A conversation, a song, a game, or a visit from another Jewish community can become a valuable learning experience.

This is especially important for Nasenyi, where the community continues to place strong importance on Jewish education and access to learning resources. In 2025, a Jewish educational book drive brought approximately 25 boxes of Hebrew and Jewish learning materials to the Nasenyi community, reflecting the wider effort to strengthen Jewish education.

David and Itai’s visit added another kind of educational experience: direct personal connection.

Creating Memories for the Children

The children were excited to spend time with the visitors.

They learned songs, played games, practiced Hebrew, and experienced the joy of meeting fellow Jews from another country.

These experiences can remain with children long after the visitors have returned home.

For a young person growing up in Nasenyi, meeting Jewish visitors from Israel can help demonstrate that the Jewish family extends far beyond their own village.

Building the Next Generation

Jewish education is essential to the future of the Nasenyi Jewish Community.

Teaching children Hebrew, Torah, Jewish traditions, songs, and history helps preserve Jewish identity for future generations.

Visits such as this one therefore have significance beyond the few days that guests spend in the community.

They create relationships.

They inspire children.

And they remind the younger generation that they are part of a much larger Jewish world.

We thank David and Itai for giving our children their time, knowledge, friendship, and smiles.

Their visit has become another beautiful chapter in the story of Jewish learning at Nasenyi.
